Um that's because mirrors try to enforce this idea of like this this linear order the log's supposed to go one after the other. And so if I show a a mirror a fork um then the mirror is going to start refusing to to cosign any new versions of the log unless they are continuations of that same fork that we decided was a mistake and that we don't actually want to continue anymore. So before a CA was just one log and now a CA is a series of several logs that you go through in sequence. Um and that's meant to to correspond kind of roughly to this idea of you know before CAS had one chance to run their log correctly and uh now they have several chances. So if they mess up on generation one, they can move on to generation two and if they mess up on generation two, they can move on to generation three and keep going like that. Uh the the issue here and the reason why I have been kind of critical of this approach is because it has this attitude of like if a log forks then we have to throw it away because it's it's garbage and it's not useful anymore. Um and I don't think that's really true. like people could have been and probably were shown certificates that ended up on this fork. And even if the plan is to immediately revoke all of the certificates, those certificates were still issued and they were still used. And because of that, I think that they should probably still be subject to the same transparency guarantees as all of the other certificates in our system. When a CT log misbehaves, you just immediately disqualify it. Um, but a log in CT is not really analogous to how a log works in Merkel certificates. So like in certificate transparency when a CA messes up you don't have to immediately distrust the CA because you can say well everything is logged and published and so we can make it right you know that's why we built the whole CT ecosystem is so that when CA mess up we can correct it in a reasonable way but when a CT log messes up you lose the guarantee that everything is logged and published and so that's why you have to trust the log. So when a ZA messes up, you can say everything is published, we know what it is. When a log in CT messes up, you can no longer say everything is published and we know what it is. Um, and so going back to Merkel trace certificates, uh, the role that logs used to do in CT is now what mirrors do. So it's the mirror's job to make sure that everything is published. And so when CA mess up, the mirrors are what's there to help you recover. Um, and so when the CA messes up, it's not like you have to throw the whole thing away. you can use you can rely on the mirrors to get back to a good state uh and to kind of justify why that might be important to be able to recover from a forked log. Uh so when you have certificates that get issued on a fork and then you kind of just decide we're going to leave them on this fork um those certificates are a lot more likely to be missed by monitors. So if the monitor is not capable of ingesting forks, which could happen um because generally we don't expect forks. Um it could also happen that that certificates are missed if uh a fork is in a mirror that was trusted relatively recently. So maybe the monitor just doesn't know about that mirror yet and so that mirror gets shown to fork view. The monitor never knows to go look at that and it never sees those certificates. Um so it's kind of worth reflecting on to improve this we can we can ask ourel what's the property that we actually want from locks and [clears throat] uh it's easiest just to say well okay we want logs that keep all of this data in a perfect line like kind of how we traditionally understood CT logs but that property itself is not really what we care about uh what we care about is this idea that everybody can see everything that's been submitted to a log book and those two things are not really the same. Like keeping data in a perfect line, having this linearizability property uh is a really helpful tool that can help make sure that everybody sees everything that's been submitted, but it's not itself the goal. And so if we say, you know, okay, we can let go of this property that everything has to be in a perfect line, what can we actually do? Uh well, we can do something called reconciliation. And reconciliation is this idea that you know if a log presents one fork to one mirror and a different fork to a different mirror, the log should be able to merge those two different views so that the mirrors agree again. And the way that you would do that is something like this. Um where we have our fork and then you know basically we just take the certificates from and we pop them onto the end of the other fork. And now everybody is is happy because uh everybody can see the same certificates again. Both of the mirrors agree again. And so these mirrors are essentially useful. They can both be used equally and uh everybody knows everything that's been issued. Uh and you may be thinking to yourself, isn't this just git rebase? And yes, it is. And that is actually the totality of my argument that this is not an insane idea. There's precedent. So, how could it possibly be insane? You maybe even did it today. Um, and more specifically like implementation wise, uh, how we would implement the sort of rebase or like reconciliation idea. Well, from mirrors a perspective, from mirror A's perspective, who saw the kind of simpler version of the fork, you just submit the the certificates that were on the fork. And so, this is not special for mirror A at all. Um, mirror B is a little bit more interesting, uh, a little bit more complicated. So, mirror B, step one, mirror B has to see a fork that is, uh, inconsistent with what are other mirrors have been shown. Uh, then in step two, essentially what the log does is it goes to the mirror and it asks the mirror to go back to some kind of regressed view. Uh when this happens, uh the mirror doesn't just delete the certificates that were submitted after this point. It moves them into a backlog where they're not, you know, in the log anymore, but they are safe and the mirror still has them. Uh and then once those certificates are in the backlog, uh the log resubmits any missing certificates to the mirror that it needs. Um and it's important that you know while this backlog is non-MP, the mirror never issues any new co- signatures. And that is uh it's necessary to make sure that there is actually an incentive to empty the backlog because if the mirror was willing to keep operating in this mode, you know, maybe the backlog just never gets emptied and those certificates don't end up where people can see them. Um but yeah, and so then once we've added once we've added any kind of missing certificates that we need, uh we go through and we resubmit all of the certificates that are in the backlog, taking them kind of like a queue, resubmitting them in order. Um, and once the backlog is empty again, then you're done. This mirror is reconciled and uh the mirror can start providing co- signatures again and it has the same view as uh all of the other mirrors. So that's how it works for the mirror from a monitor's perspective. uh if a monitor happens to be, you know, crawling some mirror that goes through reconciliation, uh all it really has to do is jump back to some some common ancestor point and that can be signaled through like an API with the mirror and then start crawling again. Um and that obviously does result in processing the same certificate multiple times, but you get this really nice guarantee that uh every certificate that's been issued on any fork your monitor will see at least once. Um, and monitors can also either trust the mirror to do reconciliation correctly. Um, which is kind of everybody trusts the mirror to do reconciliation correctly because that's his job. But the monitor can also check that reconciliation was done with a typical kind of consistency proof. Um, so that's also pretty easy. Um, so to to recap and to kind of fully compare this with the idea of like we're just going to throw the log away if it ever is operated incorrectly and we're going to move on to the next generation. Um, I think the reconciliation significantly simplifies monitor implementation. So with the log generation idea, uh essentially each mirror could potentially be shown a different fork and monitors need to be able to essentially look at every single mirror, identify if a mirror has been shown a fork and then identify where the fork happens, go through and crawl that fork from that mirror specifically and like have some way to represent forks internally. That can all be relatively complicated. Uh whereas with reconciliation logs are essentially always in a linear order from the monitor's perspect from the monitor's perspective. It's just that sometimes the the monitor has to go back and start over a little bit. Um but uh it's always in a linear order and also it doesn't matter which mirror the the monitor actually uses. You can call any line any mirror and as long as they all end up reconciled in the end, the monitor will see every certificate. Um reconciliation also ensures that forks are mirrored equally as well. So with uh if we're just going to leave kind of forks out in the world uh then certificates may exist only on one fork that's only in one specific mirror and it's uh more likely to be lost or deleted. Um whereas with reconciliation if you issue a certificate on a fork that certificate just gets you know put back into every other mirror gets put back into the same view that every other mirror sees. And so that is is guaranteed to last a little bit longer. Uh and then the third thing is that reconciliation makes monitors more resilient to still configuration. So that's what I talked about a little bit before where if uh a if a new mirror becomes trusted and the monitor doesn't [clears throat] know about it yet. Um then any certificates on a fork sent to that mirror specifically the monitor will not know about. It won't see them. Uh and so those would be missed. Whereas with reconciliation, even if a fork is sent to an unknown mirror, if that unknown mirror is reconciled with the known mirrors, then our monitor will still see it. Um, so that's quite nice.
